items.title: L6: How panels score one answer
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles guidance; Civil Service Jobs recruitment guidance
items.body: Panel members usually score each behaviour or strength separately, using the descriptors for the grade being recruited. Scoring is often on a numerical scale, commonly 1 to 7, where middle scores mean the evidence was acceptable and the top scores mean strong, convincing evidence. Each panel member normally takes notes while you speak and decides a score independently. The panel then compares scores and agrees a final one, sometimes called moderation. Scores rest on the evidence you give in the room, not on your CV, your reputation or the impression you gave in the previous question. Evidence scores well when it is specific (what you personally did), relevant (it matches the behaviour asked) and shows an outcome. It scores poorly when it is vague, generic ('I always...'), about what the team did rather than you, or about what you would do in theory. A panel cannot credit something you thought but did not say, so a good action left unspoken earns nothing. Panels are trained to avoid the halo effect, where one strong answer lifts later scores, and to avoid comparing you with the previous candidate; each person is scored against the criteria, not against other candidates. Scores across behaviours are usually added up and candidates ranked, with offers made from the top down, subject to a minimum pass mark.

questions.prompt: A candidate describes an excellent result but never says what they personally did. Why will the answer probably score low?

options.text: Results mentioned before the actions are marked down by convention
Answers that spend time on outcomes lose marks under the scoring rules
Panels only mark the actions described and ignore results altogether
There is no evidence of the candidate's own contribution

questions.hint: Scores rest on what you personally did, not just on the outcome.

questions.prompt: Why does each panel member usually decide a score independently before the panel compares?

options.text: So the panel can avoid writing any notes
So one forceful panel member does not sway the others
So scores can be taken straight from the candidate's CV
So candidates can see their score straight away

questions.hint: Independent scoring protects against one view dominating.

questions.prompt: What are panel scores normally judged against?

options.text: The behaviour descriptors for the grade
How long the candidate has worked in their current field
The chair's view of what a good employee looks like
The standard shown by the other candidates seen that day

questions.hint: Each answer is measured against the criteria for the role, not against people.

questions.prompt: A panel member gives a weak answer a high score because the previous answer was brilliant. What is this bias called?

options.text: Probing
Moderation
The halo effect
Positive discrimination

questions.hint: A strong earlier impression spills into later scores.

questions.prompt: You thought of a very good action during a story but did not say it aloud. What credit will it get?

options.text: Half credit, if the CV mentions similar work
Full credit, since the panel can infer it from the story
None, because the panel can only score what it hears
Credit only if you mention it at the end of the interview

questions.hint: Unspoken actions are invisible to the panel.

questions.prompt: Which statement would a panel find the strongest evidence for Managing a Quality Service?

options.text: 'Three forms came back with the same missing date, so I added a prompt to our checklist and returns fell.'
'Our team has a strong reputation for quality, which I helped to maintain by working hard every day.'
'I always make sure the quality of everything I produce is of a high standard, and colleagues know it.'
'If I had more time I would check every form twice, because accuracy is vital in this kind of work.'

questions.hint: Specific, personal, and shows an outcome.

questions.prompt: A candidate with an impressive CV gives vague answers in the interview. What is the most likely result?

options.text: High scores, because the panel will already be aware of their background
Low scores, as the interview evidence is what is marked
The CV is scored in place of the interview answers in that case
Scores raised to match the strength of the CV at the moderation stage

questions.hint: CV reputation does not replace interview evidence.

questions.prompt: A panel member says 'the last candidate gave a much better answer, so this is only a 3.' What is wrong with this?

options.text: A score of 3 is not permitted until the panel has agreed it unanimously
Nothing, because panels are meant to rank each person against the one before
Scores should only be given once every candidate has been seen
Candidates should be scored against the criteria, not each other

questions.hint: Comparison with another candidate is not the marking standard.

questions.prompt: What does 'moderation' usually mean at the end of an interview?

options.text: The candidate is asked to moderate their own answers
The panel rounds every score down to the nearest whole number
The panel compares individual scores and agrees a final score
A manager outside the panel decides the final score alone

questions.hint: Moderation is the agreement of final scores.

questions.prompt: After all interviews, how are offers usually made?

options.text: In the order in which candidates first applied
To the candidate the chair felt had the best personality
To every candidate above the pass mark at the same moment
From the top of the ranked list downwards, above a pass mark

questions.hint: Ranking by score decides the order of offers.

items.title: L6: Spotting what is missing in an answer
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles guidance; Civil Service Jobs STAR method guidance
items.body: A complete behaviour answer has four parts, often called STAR: Situation, Task, Action and Result. Strong panels are usually listening for two things most of all: your Action, in detail, and your Result, with evidence it worked. A common gap is the missing Result. The candidate explains what they did and then stops, so the panel cannot tell whether it made any difference. A second gap is a missing Task: the answer describes a busy time but never says what you were responsible for. A third is the Action that hides inside 'we': 'we reviewed the process' does not tell the panel what you contributed. A fourth is a Situation that takes up most of the time, leaving 20 seconds for the Action. As a rough guide, keep context to about a fifth of the answer and spend most of the time on the Action and Result. A fifth gap is relevance: a good story that shows a different behaviour from the one asked scores poorly, because panels mark the behaviour in the question. When you listen to an answer, ask four things. What was the person responsible for? What exactly did they do? What changed as a result? Does that match the behaviour asked about? Whichever answer is missing is the one a follow-up question will usually go after.

questions.prompt: A candidate describes reorganising a shared drive in detail but says nothing about what changed afterwards. What is missing?

options.text: The Action
The Result
The Situation
The Task

questions.hint: The panel cannot tell whether the work made a difference.

questions.prompt: 'We reviewed the process and we cut the delays.' What is the main weakness?

options.text: It does not show what the candidate personally did
It spends too much time on the outcome of the work
It describes a situation that is too short to follow
It mentions delays, which are a negative subject for a panel

questions.hint: 'We' hides the individual Action.

questions.prompt: A candidate spends two minutes describing the busy office and 20 seconds on what they did. What is the problem?

options.text: The answer included a Result as well as an Action
Too many figures were used when describing the office
Too much time on the Situation, too little on the Action
The Task was explained more than once in the answer

questions.hint: Most of the time should go on Action and Result.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much of a STAR answer should be taken up by the context, as a rough guide?

options.text: None, context should be skipped
About a fifth
About three quarters
About half

questions.hint: Keep the setting short so the Action and Result can be developed.

questions.prompt: You are asked for a time you changed something for the better. A candidate describes a good example of staying calm under pressure. Why does it score badly?

options.text: It shows a different behaviour from the one asked
Staying calm is never relevant to a Civil Service role
The panel only scores stories about teamwork
The candidate should have mentioned nerves

questions.hint: Panels mark the behaviour in the question.

questions.prompt: A candidate says 'I was in charge of making sure the weekly report went out on time, and there were four people sending me data.' Which STAR part is this?

options.text: Action
Result
Reflection
Task

questions.hint: It states what the candidate was responsible for.

questions.prompt: Which listener question would most directly find a missing Task?

options.text: What was this person responsible for?
What would they do differently next time?
How long ago did the story happen?
How many colleagues were involved in it?

questions.hint: The Task is the personal responsibility in the story.

questions.prompt: Which part of a weak answer is a follow-up question most likely to target?

options.text: The part the candidate explained in most detail
Whichever part was left out or left vague
The candidate's stated reason for applying
The opening sentence of the answer

questions.hint: Probes usually fill the gaps.

questions.prompt: 'It went well and everyone was happy.' What is missing from this Result?

options.text: A reference to the interview panel
A mention of the department's name
Evidence of what actually changed
A longer description of the Situation

questions.hint: A good Result is specific and concrete.

questions.prompt: Mid-answer you realise you have not said what you personally did. What is the best move?

options.text: Stop and ask whether the panel has enough
Move straight on and hope the panel infers it
Start the story again from the beginning
Say what you did next, then give the Result

questions.hint: You can repair the answer in the moment.

items.title: L6: Choosing the strongest of three answers
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles guidance; Civil Service Jobs interview guidance
items.body: When you compare answers, whether in practice or on a training course, use the same checklist each time. First, does the answer match the behaviour asked? Second, is it one clear example rather than a list of generalities? Third, is the Action specific and personal, shown with verbs such as 'I checked', 'I agreed', 'I wrote'? Fourth, does the Result say what changed, ideally with a measure such as time saved, errors reduced or feedback received? Fifth, does it show the right level of responsibility for the grade? An Administrative Officer example is often about a task they carried out, whereas an EO or HEO example usually shows more independence, planning or influence. A stronger answer is not always the longest. A short, precise answer can beat a long one that wanders. Nor is it always the one with the biggest event: a modest example told with clear actions and a real result usually beats a dramatic story where the candidate's role is vague. Be careful with answers that sound confident but offer no evidence, such as 'I am an excellent communicator and people always say so'. Confidence alone is not an action or a result. When two answers both look good, the stronger one usually shows reasoning: why the person chose that action, what they weighed up, and what they learned from the outcome.

questions.prompt: Which check should come first when comparing three answers to a behaviour question?

options.text: Whether each answer matches the behaviour asked
Which of the three answers is the longest
Which answer describes the most dramatic event
Which candidate sounds the most confident

questions.hint: A good answer to the wrong question still scores poorly.

questions.prompt: Answer 1: 'I am an excellent communicator and people always say so.' Answer 2: 'I rewrote our rejection letter after three people phoned to ask what it meant, and calls fell.' Which is stronger and why?

options.text: Answer 1, because it shows confidence
Answer 2, because it has a specific action and result
Answer 2, because letters are more important than speaking
Answer 1, because it is shorter

questions.hint: Confidence is not evidence; actions and results are.

questions.prompt: Which verb pattern signals a strong Action?

options.text: 'We tend to, we often, we usually'
'Everyone pulled together'
'It was decided that'
'I checked, I agreed, I wrote'

questions.hint: Personal action verbs show your own contribution.

questions.prompt: A short, precise answer is compared with a long, rambling one on the same topic. What is likely?

options.text: Both receive the same score
The panel will mark only the first sentence of each
The short answer can score better if it has clearer evidence
The long answer always scores better because it has more detail

questions.hint: Length is not quality.

questions.prompt: A dramatic story leaves the candidate's own role unclear. A second candidate describes a modest task with clear actions and a measured result. Which usually scores higher?

options.text: The first, as bigger events attract extra marks
The first, as dramatic events show more skill under pressure
They score the same, since both stories are real
The second, as personal action is clear

questions.hint: Clear personal evidence beats a vague big event.

questions.prompt: Two answers both include action and result. Which is usually stronger?

options.text: The one that mentions more colleagues by role
The one that explains why the action was chosen
The one that was delivered faster
The one that uses more technical terms

questions.hint: Reasoning shows judgement.

questions.prompt: What does 'the right level of responsibility' mean when judging an answer for an EO role?

options.text: Examples from before the candidate's current job are discounted
The example must involve responsibility for a budget
Some independence, planning or influence
Only examples where the candidate managed other staff count

questions.hint: Expectations rise with grade.

questions.prompt: Which Result would a panel rate highest for a task involving a customer form?

options.text: 'Complaints about the form fell from about ten a month to two after I added a worked example.'
'It was a good learning experience for me and for the team.'
'Everyone found the new version more useful and said so.'
'My manager seemed pleased with how it all turned out.'

questions.hint: A measured change is more convincing than a general feeling.

questions.prompt: Two examples are offered for Delivering at Pace: planning a workload across a fortnight, or a single day of panic. Which probably shows more of the behaviour?

options.text: The single day, since panic shows urgency
Neither, as Delivering at Pace excludes planning
The fortnight, as it shows prioritising and tracking
They are equal if both tasks were finished

questions.hint: Delivering at Pace is about managing and prioritising work, not just urgency.

questions.prompt: Which phrase most often signals an answer that lacks evidence?

options.text: 'I sent the draft to my manager for comments.'
'I agreed a rota with three colleagues on Monday.'
'I checked the figures against last year's.'
'I always do my best to be a team player.'

questions.hint: General statements of character are not examples.

items.title: L6: When 'we' hides your contribution
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles guidance; Civil Service Jobs interview guidance
items.body: Many Civil Service examples come from teamwork, so candidates naturally say 'we'. The risk is that the panel cannot tell what you did. They are scoring you, not your team. A good approach is to use 'we' for the setting and 'I' for your contribution: 'Our team had a backlog of 300 cases. I proposed splitting them by type, drew up a simple tracker, and checked it each morning'. You do not need to claim credit for others' work. Honest wording like 'My part was...' or 'The decision was my manager's, but I gathered the figures' is perfectly acceptable and helps the panel judge your actual role. Be careful of the opposite error: claiming something that was a team effort as if it were all your own. A follow-up such as 'Who else was involved?' or 'What did the others do?' will usually expose it, and the Civil Service Code values honesty. For behaviours such as Working Together, however, the team is part of the evidence. There you should describe how you supported others, shared information or handled a disagreement, as well as the shared result. If a panel asks 'what was your role?', it is a sign they are not yet hearing it, so answer directly with the specific actions you took.

questions.prompt: What is a good way to balance 'we' and 'I' in an answer?

options.text: 'We' throughout, to show modesty
'We' for the setting, 'I' for your contribution
The passive voice, to avoid both
'I' for every part, including team decisions

questions.hint: The panel needs to hear what you did.

questions.prompt: Why is 'we' risky in a behaviour answer?

options.text: The panel is scoring you, so it must hear your own part
It makes the answer too long
Panels penalise candidates who work in teams
The word 'we' is not allowed in Civil Service interviews

questions.hint: Individual evidence is what is scored.

questions.prompt: A candidate says 'The decision was my manager's, but I gathered the figures.' How would a panel generally see this?

options.text: As a reason to set the example aside
As honest and clear about their role
As an attempt to avoid responsibility
As a sign the candidate lacks initiative

questions.hint: Being clear about your part is positive.

questions.prompt: A candidate presents a team project as entirely their own work. What is the likely outcome if the panel probes?

options.text: Nothing, because teamwork claims are not checked
The panel will ask the candidate to retake the interview
The panel will award extra marks for the confidence shown
The claim may be exposed, and it breaches honesty

questions.hint: Overclaiming is risky and dishonest.

questions.prompt: Which follow-up question most suggests the panel is not yet hearing your contribution?

options.text: What was your role in that?
When did that happen?
How many colleagues were in the room?
Where was your office?

questions.hint: Directly asks for the personal element.

questions.prompt: For Working Together, what should an answer include in addition to the shared result?

options.text: Only the tasks you completed alone
A full list of colleagues' roles and grades
How you supported others or handled disagreement
A description of your manager's strengths

questions.hint: The team is part of the evidence for this behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best separates context from personal action?

options.text: 'We split them by type and we tracked them each day.'
'The tracker was built and the cases were split by type.'
'The team had 300 cases waiting. I suggested splitting them by type and built the tracker.'
'Everyone chipped in and the backlog got done between us.'

questions.hint: It names the team situation then your actions.

questions.prompt: A candidate says 'My part was writing the guidance; others dealt with the data.' What does this do for the panel?

options.text: It makes the candidate's role clear
It suggests the candidate was not involved in the work
It makes the example irrelevant to the behaviour
It suggests the candidate needs an adjustment

questions.hint: Clear boundaries help scoring.

questions.prompt: Which wording would normally worry a panel because it hides the speaker's action?

options.text: 'I asked the team for ideas before changing the process.'
'I wrote the first draft of the new process.'
'I tested the process on five cases.'
'It was agreed that the process would change.'

questions.hint: The passive voice leaves out who did it.

questions.prompt: A colleague suggested the idea, and you then carried it out. What should you say?

options.text: Choose a different story with no ideas from others
Credit the idea and describe your part in making it happen
Present the idea as your own, since you did the work
Leave out the work and only describe the idea

questions.hint: Honesty about origin is fine; what matters is what you did.

items.title: L6: Results that are weak, missing or negative
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles guidance; Civil Service Code
items.body: Results are where many answers fall short. A weak Result is vague ('it went well'), unmeasured, or about feelings alone. A stronger one says what changed: time saved, fewer errors, a complaint resolved, a deadline met, feedback received. If the figure is not exact, an honest estimate is fine: 'about half the calls we had before' is better than nothing. Do not invent numbers; the panel may ask how you know. Some examples do not have a clean success. Panels often ask about a time something went wrong, and may also probe when your answer has no clear outcome. A negative Result can still score well if you explain what happened, what you learned and what you did differently afterwards. The best answers about mistakes own the error plainly, show how it was put right, and describe a changed habit or check. Blaming others, or presenting a mistake as a hidden strength ('I work too hard'), tends to weaken the answer. If a project outcome was not yet known, say what you can: the early feedback, the next step, or what you would measure. Where a result depended on others, you may say so, but still describe the part you can fairly claim. Learning is part of the Result for behaviours such as Developing Self and Others and Changing and Improving.

questions.prompt: Which Result gives the clearest evidence of impact on a processing queue?

options.text: 'Waiting times fell from about six weeks to about four; I checked the monthly figures.'
'It went really well and I was very pleased with it overall.'
'Everyone seemed happier afterwards, which was lovely to see.'
'My manager said thank you and told the rest of the team.'

questions.hint: A change you can measure and explain is persuasive.

questions.prompt: A candidate cannot remember the exact figure. What is the best approach?

options.text: Leave out the Result and focus on the Action
Give a precise-sounding number to avoid looking unsure
Give an honest estimate and say it is approximate
Say there was no measurable result

questions.hint: Honest estimates are fine; invention is not.

questions.prompt: A panel asks about a time you made a mistake. What makes a strong answer?

options.text: Describe a mistake made by a colleague that you corrected
Choose a mistake that turned out to have no consequences
Explain why the circumstances meant it was not really your fault
Own it, put it right, say what you do differently now

questions.hint: Ownership and learning are scored.

questions.prompt: Which is a weak way to answer a question about a weakness or mistake?

options.text: 'I missed a deadline, told my manager early and now build in a check-in.'
'My only weakness is that I work too hard.'
'I used to avoid asking questions, so I now ask on day one.'
'I once sent a draft to the wrong person and now check the address twice.'

questions.hint: Disguising a strength as a weakness lacks honesty.

questions.prompt: The outcome of your project is not yet known. What should you do?

options.text: Choose a different example, as unfinished work cannot score
Say that results do not matter for this behaviour
Describe the project as a success anyway
Describe early feedback, next steps and what you would measure

questions.hint: You can still provide evidence of progress.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to invent a figure in a Result?

options.text: The panel may ask how you know, and honesty is expected
A figure shortens the answer and loses time for the Action
Panels mark down answers that contain any numbers
Figures are only credited at senior grades

questions.hint: Invention risks being exposed and breaches the Code's honesty.

questions.prompt: For Developing Self and Others, what is often part of a strong Result?

options.text: How much money the work saved the department
How many people you managed during the work
What you learned and how you used it afterwards
How quickly the work was finished compared with others

questions.hint: Learning is the outcome the behaviour looks for.

questions.prompt: 'The project failed because the other team did not deliver.' What is the main weakness?

options.text: It uses the word 'failed', which panels avoid
It blames others and shows no learning or action
It does not name the other team involved
It is too short to be scored by a panel

questions.hint: Blame without reflection scores poorly.

questions.prompt: A result depended on several people. How should you describe it?

options.text: Claim the whole result as your own
Avoid mentioning the others involved
Say so, but describe the part you can fairly claim
Choose a story where nobody else was involved

questions.hint: Be honest and personal.

questions.prompt: Which is the best ending to a story where the plan did not work as hoped?

options.text: 'It was not my fault, as the brief kept changing.'
'It would have worked if we had been given more time.'
'It was fine in the end, and nobody complained about it.'
'It only partly worked, so I asked users what was missing and changed the next version.'

questions.hint: Shows learning and action after setback.

items.title: L6: Judging strengths-based answers
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles guidance; Civil Service Jobs strengths-based interview guidance
items.body: Strengths questions work differently from behaviour questions. They ask what you enjoy, what energises you and what you would do in a situation, rather than asking for a past example. They are often short, quick and spontaneous, and panels may ask several in a row. The aim is to find out what you naturally do well and enjoy, because people who enjoy a task tend to do it well. Panels listen for signs of genuine energy, such as natural tone, relevant examples, and a clear link to the way the role works. Typical questions are 'What do you enjoy most about helping others?' or 'Would you rather plan in detail or adapt as you go?'. Panels are not looking for one right answer. A candidate who says they prefer detailed planning can score well if they explain how it helps; one who prefers adapting can score well if they explain how they keep control. They do mark honesty and consistency. A rehearsed, over-polished answer is easy to spot. So is an answer that does not match what the candidate says in the behaviour questions. Brief, specific answers with a small example, and a bit of personality, usually work better than long speeches. Avoid choosing an answer because you think it is what the panel wants; pick what is true for you, and give the reason.

questions.prompt: How do strengths questions mainly differ from behaviour questions?

options.text: They are scored without reference to the job
They ask what you enjoy and naturally do, not for a past example
They ask for longer STAR stories about difficult periods
They are only used for senior roles

questions.hint: Strengths focus on energy and preference.

questions.prompt: What do panels listen for in strengths answers?

options.text: Genuine energy and a relevant reason
Phrases copied from the advert
The longest and most detailed answer available
Technical terms from the job description

questions.hint: Authenticity is a key signal.

questions.prompt: A strengths question asks: 'Would you rather plan in detail or adapt as you go?' What makes a good answer?

options.text: Saying you do both equally, without giving a reason
Either, if you explain honestly how it helps you
Only 'plan in detail', as the Civil Service values structure
Only 'adapt as you go', as it shows flexibility

questions.hint: There is no single correct preference.

questions.prompt: Which answer would a panel find more convincing?

options.text: 'Organising is definitely a strength I have and I use it regularly.'
'I think organisation matters a great deal in an office like this.'
'I have always been a person who loves to organise everything around me.'
'I enjoy sorting out muddled records; last week I tidied a shared folder and everyone found things faster.'

questions.hint: A small example gives the answer substance.

questions.prompt: Why can an over-polished, rehearsed strengths answer weaken your score?

options.text: It suggests the candidate has not read the advert
It makes the answer too short to be scored
It can sound unnatural and hide real preferences
Panels penalise any preparation before the interview

questions.hint: Strengths questions aim at spontaneity.

questions.prompt: A candidate says they love working alone, then describes enjoying team brainstorming. What might the panel note?

options.text: An inconsistency worth probing
A reason to stop the strengths section
A well-balanced profile that needs no more questions
Proof the candidate is being dishonest

questions.hint: Consistency between answers matters.

questions.prompt: Why might a panel ask several strengths questions in quick succession?

options.text: To reward the candidate who speaks fastest
To get natural responses before overthinking sets in
To test how well the candidate remembers earlier answers
To shorten the interview by half

questions.hint: Speed encourages spontaneity.

questions.prompt: How long should a typical strengths answer usually be?

options.text: Under a minute, with a small example
A single word, as strengths are instinctive
At least four minutes, to show depth
As long as a full STAR story

questions.hint: Short and specific works best.

questions.prompt: Which approach to a strengths question is unwise?

options.text: Using a brief real example
Giving a short honest answer with a reason
Choosing the answer you think the panel wants
Pausing for a moment before replying

questions.hint: Honesty is part of the scoring.

questions.prompt: A candidate answers 'What energises you?' with 'Finishing a tricky task that others have left.' What would the panel probably do next?

options.text: End that section of the interview
Move straight to scoring without further questions
Ask the candidate to give a full three-part STAR story
Ask what they enjoy about it or how they approach it

questions.hint: Panels often follow up to explore the reason.

items.title: L6: Realistic panel moments and how to respond
items.source: Civil Service Jobs interview guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles guidance
items.body: Panels are normally friendly but follow a script, so some moments can feel unexpected. A panel member may say very little, write constantly, or show no reaction. This is usually because they are recording your answer and must stay neutral; it does not mean you are doing badly. Do not read their face as feedback and keep going with your answer. A panel member may interrupt politely to move you on, for example 'Thank you, can we move on to the next question?'. Panels have a fixed number of questions and time. Accept it calmly; you do not have to argue for more time. If you realise afterwards that you missed something, you can often add it later if there is a natural opening such as 'Is there anything else you would like to add?'. A panel member may ask you to repeat or clarify. That is normal and not a sign of failure. If you do not understand a question, you may ask for it to be repeated or rephrased. If a question includes jargon or a phrase you do not know, say what you understand by it, rather than guessing silently. Some panels also ask a follow-up that sounds challenging, such as 'Why did you not do it differently?'. This is a probe to understand your reasoning. Answer calmly and honestly, explaining what you knew at the time. Treat each question as a fresh start, because scores are given question by question.

questions.prompt: A panel member writes constantly and shows no reaction. What is the most sensible assumption?

options.text: They are recording and staying neutral
Your answers are going badly
They have already decided to reject you
They have lost interest in your answers

questions.hint: Neutral faces are part of fair interviewing.

questions.prompt: A panel member says 'Thank you, can we move on?' while you are mid-story. What is the best response?

options.text: Say that you had not been given enough time
Accept it calmly and take the next question
Ask to return to your story at the end
Politely insist on finishing your story

questions.hint: Time is fixed; the panel is managing it.

questions.prompt: At the end, the panel asks if you want to add anything. You missed a point earlier. What should you do?

options.text: Repeat your whole first answer in full
Explain that the panel did not ask you properly
Briefly add it, linking it to the relevant question
Say nothing, as the questions are over

questions.hint: This is a natural opening to add evidence.

questions.prompt: You do not understand a question. What is the best action?

options.text: Say the question seems unfair
Make your best guess and answer it
Use your best-prepared story that is close to it
Ask for it to be repeated or rephrased

questions.hint: Clarification is allowed and normal.

questions.prompt: A question uses a term you do not recognise. What is the best approach?

options.text: Decline to answer the question
Act as if you know it and answer in general terms
Say what you understand by it and answer on that basis
Move the discussion to a topic you know better

questions.hint: Honest interpretation is better than silent guessing.

questions.prompt: A panel member asks, 'Why did you not do it differently?' What are they most likely doing?

options.text: Preparing to mark your answer down
Probing your reasoning at the time
Signalling that your answer has ended
Telling you that your action was wrong

questions.hint: Challenge is often probing, not criticism.

questions.prompt: How are scores usually given?

options.text: Question by question
By averaging all candidates
Based on your first answer alone
Only at the end based on a single impression

questions.hint: Each answer is a fresh chance.

questions.prompt: You feel your last answer went badly. What should you do before the next question?

options.text: Apologise for the last answer before moving on
Ask the panel how that answer went
Keep the next answer short to limit damage
Take a breath and treat the next question as fresh

questions.hint: Scores are separate; recover and move on.

questions.prompt: A panel member asks you to repeat part of your answer. What does this probably mean?

options.text: The answer has been marked as a failure
They missed a detail and want to record it accurately
They are testing your patience
The interview will now be stopped

questions.hint: It is routine.

questions.prompt: A panel member frowns during your answer. What is a reasonable reaction?

options.text: Change your answer to try to please them
Assume the answer is wrong and wrap up quickly
Carry on and finish clearly
Stop and ask what is wrong

questions.hint: Facial expressions are not scores.

items.title: L6: Video interview problems in realistic settings
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance on interview formats; GOV.UK
items.body: Many Civil Service interviews are held by video, so panel members and candidates both need to handle technical hiccups. If your connection freezes, stay calm, turn your camera off briefly to save bandwidth if appropriate, and rejoin or phone the contact number in your invitation. Panels know technology fails and they are generally flexible, provided you tell them quickly. If the panel is late, wait patiently; use the contact details if they have not joined after a few minutes. If there is a noise in the background, such as a doorbell or a child, apologise briefly and carry on. You do not need to over-explain. If you cannot hear a question, say so straight away rather than guessing. If you are asked to share your screen, such as in a presentation, check beforehand that you can, and close other windows containing private information. Look at the camera lens when you speak, not your own image, to create eye contact. Place notes where you can glance without turning your head, and only if the invitation said they are allowed. Sitting slightly back, with your face and shoulders in frame, helps. Keep a charger plugged in and your phone on silent. At the end, do not hang up before the panel says the meeting is over, and leave the call properly, not by shutting the laptop abruptly.

questions.prompt: Your connection freezes mid-answer. What is the most sensible first move?

options.text: Email each panel member after the interview
Wait on the frozen screen until the panel gets in touch
Abandon the interview and apply for another vacancy
Try to rejoin, and ring the contact number if that fails

questions.hint: Telling the panel promptly is key.

questions.prompt: The panel has not joined five minutes after the start time. What should you do?

options.text: Use the contact details in the invitation
Wait indefinitely without contacting anyone
Leave the call at once and reapply
Start without them

questions.hint: Contact the recruitment team if no one arrives.

questions.prompt: A doorbell rings during your answer. What is the best response?

options.text: Stop the interview and leave
Apologise briefly and carry on
Ignore the question and answer the door
Make a long apology

questions.hint: A short apology is enough.

questions.prompt: You cannot hear a question clearly. What should you do?

options.text: Wait until the end and then mention it
Answer a similar question you have prepared for
Guess what was asked and answer that
Say so straight away and ask for it to be repeated

questions.hint: Better to ask than answer the wrong question.

questions.prompt: You are asked to share your screen for a presentation. What should you do beforehand?

options.text: Test sharing, and close windows showing private information
Ask the panel to test it at the start of the session
Nothing until the panel asks, since they will help
Open all your emails so you can show them if needed

questions.hint: Prevents embarrassment and privacy problems.

questions.prompt: Where should you look to create eye contact on video?

options.text: At your own image
At the panel's faces on screen
At the camera lens
At the ceiling

questions.hint: Looking at the lens feels like eye contact.

questions.prompt: When are notes appropriate during a video interview?

options.text: Always, as full scripts to read aloud
Only when hidden from the panel's view
Never, whatever the invitation says
If the invitation allows them, kept where you can glance without turning away

questions.hint: Follow the guidance and use brief notes.

questions.prompt: At the end of a video interview, what should you do?

options.text: Close the laptop as soon as the last answer is given
Wait for the panel to close the meeting, then leave properly
Hang up the moment you have answered the last question
Stay connected until the recruitment team confirms the outcome

questions.hint: Leave politely when the panel indicates the end.

questions.prompt: What helps a panel see you clearly on video?

options.text: A lamp shining at the camera
Sitting very close to the lens
A plain background, with your face and shoulders in frame
A bright window directly behind you

questions.hint: Visibility and simplicity matter.

questions.prompt: Which of these reduces interruptions during a video interview?

options.text: Silencing your phone and closing other applications
Keeping notifications on in case the panel messages you
Playing quiet music to keep calm
Keeping a second call open as a backup

questions.hint: Prevents distracting alerts.

items.title: L6: Honesty, confidentiality and the Civil Service Code in examples
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; GOV.UK
items.body: The Civil Service Code sets out four values: integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. Panels expect your interview to show them. Honesty means describing what you did truthfully, without inflating your role or making up results. Integrity includes not misusing information you hold. Confidentiality matters when you draw examples from a current or previous job. You may describe the situation in general terms but must not reveal personal data, names of clients, or sensitive or classified information. For example, you can say 'I helped a customer who was upset about a delayed payment' without naming them, or discussing their case. If you cannot explain an example without breaching confidentiality, choose another. If a panel asks for names or details that would disclose confidential material, politely say you cannot share them, and explain the substance in general terms. Objectivity and impartiality are relevant when you describe decisions: you should base them on evidence and treat people fairly. Candidates sometimes describe cutting corners or ignoring a rule to get work done. Even if the outcome was good, this can weaken your answer because it shows poor judgement against the Code. If you describe a time you raised a concern about something wrong, you can score well; it shows integrity. Remember also that the Code does not require you to be perfect, but it does require you to be honest about your actions.

questions.prompt: Which four values are set out in the Civil Service Code?

options.text: Courage, pride, speed, loyalty
Integrity, honesty, objectivity, impartiality
Efficiency, secrecy, loyalty, accuracy
Fairness, leadership, flexibility, teamwork

questions.hint: These are the Code's core values.

questions.prompt: You are describing a time you helped an upset customer. What should you avoid?

options.text: Saying that the customer was upset
Describing what you said to calm them
Telling the panel the outcome of the case
Naming them or giving personal details

questions.hint: Personal data must not be disclosed.

questions.prompt: A panel asks for the name of the client in your example. What is the best response?

options.text: Say you can only answer questions about other examples
Offer to write the name down after the interview
Politely decline and explain the substance in general terms
Give the name to prove the story is real

questions.hint: Protect confidentiality while still answering.

questions.prompt: Your best example involves sensitive information you could not disclose. What is wise?

options.text: Pick an example you can describe openly
Give the details anyway, as the panel is trusted
Describe it vaguely and hope it still scores
Explain that you cannot answer this question at all

questions.hint: Better to keep to the Code.

questions.prompt: A candidate describes ignoring a safety rule to meet a deadline, with a good outcome. How might a panel see it?

options.text: As poor judgement despite the outcome
As proof of honesty and openness
As irrelevant, since the outcome was good
As initiative that deserves top marks

questions.hint: Cutting corners conflicts with the values.

questions.prompt: A candidate describes raising a concern about something wrong in their workplace. How might a panel view this?

options.text: As disloyalty to their employer
As irrelevant to the behaviour asked
As a reason to doubt their reliability
As evidence of integrity

questions.hint: Speaking up shows integrity.

questions.prompt: What does honesty mean in an interview?

options.text: Revealing everything you know about your employer
Never mentioning mistakes you made
Describing what you did truthfully, without inflating role or results
Being openly critical of colleagues

questions.hint: It means accuracy about yourself.

questions.prompt: Which example shows impartiality?

options.text: Putting off a complaint from someone who was rude
Handling requests in the order received, whoever sent them
Giving priority to requests from friends in other teams
Dealing first with requests from people you get on with

questions.hint: Impartiality means fair, evidence-based treatment.

questions.prompt: How does the Civil Service Code treat a mistake you describe at interview?

options.text: It should be left out of any example you give
It expects honesty about what you did and what you learned
It is acceptable only if someone else caused it
It counts against you whatever you learned afterwards

questions.hint: Mistakes are fine if honestly described.

questions.prompt: A candidate inflates the size of a project to impress. What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The panel will not notice the detail
The panel will give extra marks for scale
The panel will shorten the interview
A follow-up can expose it, and it breaches honesty

questions.hint: Probing questions test claims.

items.title: L6: Why this job and other opening questions
items.source: Civil Service Jobs interview guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles guidance
items.body: Interviews often begin with an opening question such as 'Why do you want this role?' or 'What do you know about our department?'. These are not scored in all competitions, but they set the tone and may be marked under Experience or Strengths. A strong answer to 'Why this job?' has three parts: what attracts you to the work itself, why this department, and what you bring. For example, you might mention a part of the department's published work, a skill that matches the advert, and a reason you care about the outcome. Avoid answers that rely only on pay, location or convenience, or on a general wish for stability. These may be true but they do not show that you understand the work. Do not recite the department's website. Choose two or three points that really interest you, and link them to the role. If you are asked 'Where do you see yourself in five years?', answer honestly and constructively: you can mention wanting to develop skills, take on more responsibility and contribute in this or a related area. You do not have to promise to stay for ever. If the advert covers a particular grade, show you understand its scope: do not describe a job two grades higher. When asked for a summary of your background, keep it to about a minute, concentrate on the parts relevant to the role, and end with why you applied.

questions.prompt: What are the three parts of a strong answer to 'Why this job?'

options.text: Your five-year plan, your hobbies and your family
Pay, location and working hours
The work, the department, and what you bring
A history of every job you have held

questions.hint: Links your motivation to the role.

questions.prompt: Which reason alone is weakest for 'Why do you want this role?'

options.text: 'It is close to home and the pay is steady.'
'The role uses my experience of working with the public.'
'I have followed the department's work on a policy I care about.'
'I want to build my skills in casework.'

questions.hint: Convenience does not show understanding of the work.

questions.prompt: How should you use what you know about the department?

options.text: Pick two or three points and link them to the role
Recite as much of the website as you can
Criticise its recent work to show insight
Avoid mentioning the department, as the panel knows it

questions.hint: Depth beats quantity.

questions.prompt: How should you answer 'Where do you see yourself in five years?'

options.text: Say you don't plan ahead
Promise to stay in the same post indefinitely
Say you want the panel's own jobs
Honestly, mentioning growth in skills and responsibility

questions.hint: It shows ambition and realism.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with describing a job two grades above the one advertised?

options.text: It shows ambition and is always rewarded
The panel requires it to assess potential
It suggests you misunderstand the scope of the role
It breaches the Civil Service Code

questions.hint: Show you understand the grade.

questions.prompt: How long should a summary of your background usually be?

options.text: Ten minutes
About a minute
Ten seconds
As long as your CV

questions.hint: Brevity and relevance matter.

questions.prompt: What should a background summary end with?

options.text: An apology for any gaps
Why you applied
A list of hobbies
Your salary expectations

questions.hint: Link back to the role.

questions.prompt: Opening questions are not always scored. What is true?

options.text: They cannot be prepared for in advance
They can safely be answered casually
They are never relevant to the final score
They still shape first impressions and may be marked under other criteria

questions.hint: Do not treat them as casual.

questions.prompt: A candidate says 'I want stability.' How could they strengthen this?

options.text: Link it to building a career in public service
Add that they dislike risk
Say no more, since it is honest
Mention that they have no other offers

questions.hint: Connect motivation to the role.

questions.prompt: Why is it unhelpful to recite the department's website?

options.text: Panels dislike candidates using websites
It breaks interview rules about research
It shows you read it, not that you understand the work
It uses up too little of the interview time

questions.hint: Choose what matters to you.

items.title: L6: Questions to ask and closing well
items.source: Civil Service Jobs interview guidance; GOV.UK
items.body: Many interviews close with 'Do you have any questions for us?'. This is usually not scored, but it leaves a final impression and can help you decide if the job suits you. Good questions are about the work and team: what a typical week looks like, how new starters are supported, what the team's priorities are over the next year, or how performance is reviewed. Avoid asking about things the advert already answers, or questions that focus only on holidays, leave or how quickly you can get promoted. Questions about pay may be better left until an offer is made, as the advert normally gives the pay range. Do not ask the panel how you did, as they cannot say. If you have an adjustment or a practical question, such as when you will hear, ask it. You may prepare two or three questions in case some are answered during the interview, and it is fine to say 'You have covered most of my questions already'. If asked 'Is there anything else you would like to add?', use it to give one point of evidence you missed, or briefly restate why you are a good fit, in thirty seconds. Close by thanking the panel. After the interview, it is acceptable to wait for the outcome; chasing the panel individually is not usually appropriate.

questions.prompt: Which question is most suitable to ask at the end?

options.text: 'What would a typical week look like in this team?'
'Can you tell me how I did today?'
'How many days of leave would I be entitled to?'
'How quickly can someone be promoted here?'

questions.hint: Questions about the work show interest.

questions.prompt: Which question is best avoided at the end?

options.text: One about how performance is reviewed
One about the team's priorities this year
One the advert already answers
One about how new starters are supported

questions.hint: Shows you didn't read the advert.

questions.prompt: Why should you not ask the panel how you did?

options.text: Panels are forbidden from speaking to candidates
It is considered a discourteous question
They will mark you down for asking
They cannot say, as scores are agreed afterwards

questions.hint: Scores are moderated later.

questions.prompt: When is pay usually best discussed?

options.text: It should never be discussed
After an offer, as the advert normally gives the range
At the start of the interview
At every stage of the process

questions.hint: Pay is normally set out in the advert.

questions.prompt: The panel has already covered all your prepared questions. What is acceptable?

options.text: Say they have already been covered
Ask the same question again
Say nothing and wait
Invent a question to look interested

questions.hint: No need to invent a question.

questions.prompt: 'Is there anything else you would like to add?' What is a good use of the opening?

options.text: Apologise for how you think it went
Repeat your whole last answer
Give one missed piece of evidence or restate your fit
Ask the panel for your score

questions.hint: Add value in about thirty seconds.

questions.prompt: How many questions is it sensible to prepare for the end?

options.text: Ten or more
Two or three
One only, which you must ask whatever happens
None, since asking is optional and rarely helps

questions.hint: Enough, but not excessive.

questions.prompt: After the interview, what is appropriate?

options.text: Phone the chair for an early decision
Post publicly about the panel's questions
Email each panel member to ask how you did
Wait for the outcome and respond to any messages

questions.hint: Respect the process.

questions.prompt: Why is 'When will I hear?' a reasonable question to ask?

options.text: It is practical and helps you plan
It is not permitted
It guarantees an earlier decision
It shows you expect special treatment

questions.hint: Practical questions are fine.

questions.prompt: What does a final thank-you to the panel normally show?

options.text: That you want to end quickly
Courtesy and professionalism
That you are desperate
That the panel should reward you

questions.hint: Good manners leave a positive final impression.

items.title: L6: Reading your results and feedback
items.source: Civil Service Jobs recruitment guidance; GOV.UK
items.body: After a Civil Service interview, you will usually be told if you were successful, placed on a reserve list, or unsuccessful. Reserve lists contain candidates who met the standard but were not among the top scorers, and who may be offered a post if one becomes available, often within a set time such as 6 or 12 months, as stated in the outcome. Check how long yours lasts. Offers are normally conditional: pre-employment checks such as identity, right to work, employment history references, and the Baseline Personnel Security Standard must be passed before a start date is confirmed. Some roles require further security clearance. Most departments will provide feedback on request, and many provide it automatically. Good feedback usually mentions your scores for each behaviour and the panel's comments on strengths and areas to develop. Read it carefully and look for patterns across several questions rather than single comments. If one behaviour scored low, ask yourself whether you chose the wrong example, left out the Action, or gave too little on the Result. If you disagree with the outcome you may raise a concern through the department's recruitment complaint process, which is set out in the Civil Service Recruitment Principles; you can also ask the recruitment team if you feel a process was not followed fairly. Use feedback to build a stronger bank of examples before your next application, and thank the panel for it.

questions.prompt: What does a reserve list contain after a competition?

options.text: Staff who have resigned and may return
Candidates who failed and may reapply immediately
Candidates who met the standard and may be offered a post if one arises
Panel members available as substitutes

questions.hint: They are held in case of vacancies.

questions.prompt: An outcome email says you are on a reserve list. What should you check?

options.text: Who sits on the panel
Whether the job has been renamed
Nothing, it lasts for ever
How long the list lasts

questions.hint: The period is usually stated.

questions.prompt: A job offer is described as 'conditional'. What does that mean?

options.text: It will be withdrawn if you ask questions about it
It lasts for a probation period of one week only
It depends on another candidate declining the post
It depends on you passing pre-employment checks

questions.hint: Checks must be passed before the start date.

questions.prompt: Which is a usual pre-employment check?

options.text: A fitness test
Identity and right to work
A standardised numeracy test
A driving test for every role

questions.hint: These are standard.

questions.prompt: What does the Baseline Personnel Security Standard involve?

options.text: A psychometric assessment
A review of social media posts
Verifying identity, right to work, employment history and unspent convictions
A full medical examination

questions.hint: It is a baseline set of checks.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to read interview feedback?

options.text: Look for patterns across questions
Focus on the harshest single comment
Argue the case for each point
Ignore it, since it only reflects one panel

questions.hint: Patterns show what to change.

questions.prompt: One behaviour received a low score. What should you ask yourself?

options.text: Whether the job was fair to apply for
Whether you should give up applying
Whether the example, Action or Result was the weak part
Whether the panel disliked you

questions.hint: Diagnose using the STAR elements.

questions.prompt: If you think the process was not followed fairly, what can you do?

options.text: Use the department's recruitment complaint process
Take no action, as the decision cannot be examined
Contact the Prime Minister's office directly
Post a public complaint naming the panel

questions.hint: A formal process exists.

questions.prompt: What do the Civil Service Recruitment Principles require of recruitment?

options.text: Selection by seniority in the department
Selection by a draw among those who pass
Selection by recommendation from managers
Selection on merit, in fair and open competition

questions.hint: Merit and open competition.

questions.prompt: How can you use feedback after an unsuccessful interview?

options.text: Reuse the same answers with more confidence
Build a stronger bank of examples
Ask for the panel's private notes
Stop applying for similar posts

questions.hint: Feedback guides improvement.

items.title: L6: Presentations and exercises at interview
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles guidance
items.body: Some Civil Service interviews include a short presentation or exercise as well as questions. These are more common above entry level, though some AO and EO competitions use them. You may be given a topic in advance or on the day, with preparation time, and asked to present for a set number of minutes, followed by questions. Panels are looking for the behaviours the exercise is designed to test, often Communicating and Influencing, Making Effective Decisions, or Seeing the Big Picture. They are not usually looking for specialist knowledge unless it is a technical role. A simple structure helps: begin with a short introduction saying what you will cover, give two or three clear points with evidence, and finish with a conclusion or recommendation. Time yourself during practice and plan to finish a little under the limit, because panels may stop you at the time limit. If using slides, keep them minimal: slides support you, they do not replace you. Check the instructions for whether visual aids are allowed. Expect questions afterwards that test your reasoning, such as 'What are the risks of that option?' or 'Who would you consult?'. It is fine to say you would need more information, if you explain what you would gather and why. Anyone who needs adjustments, for example extra preparation time, should ask in advance.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour is a presentation exercise most likely to test?

options.text: Working Together only
Managing a Quality Service only
Delivering at Pace only
Communicating and Influencing

questions.hint: Presentations show how you structure and deliver a message.

questions.prompt: What simple structure suits a short presentation?

options.text: A long story with no ending
Introduction, two or three points with evidence, conclusion
A conclusion followed by an apology
A list of facts in no set order

questions.hint: Clear structure helps the panel follow.

questions.prompt: Why plan to finish a little under the time limit?

options.text: The panel may stop you at the limit, and questions follow
It is a rule that you must finish early
Overrunning is encouraged to show detail
Panels reward the shortest talks

questions.hint: Time discipline matters.

questions.prompt: How should slides be used?

options.text: In large numbers to show effort
In place of speaking
Minimally, to support you
As a full script to read aloud

questions.hint: Slides are aids.

questions.prompt: What should you do about adjustments for a presentation, such as extra preparation time?

options.text: Ask during the presentation
Wait for the panel to notice
Skip the presentation
Ask in advance

questions.hint: Early requests allow arrangements.

questions.prompt: After your presentation you are asked 'What are the risks?' What is the panel testing?

options.text: Your memory of the slides
Your handwriting on notes
Your reasoning and judgement
Your speed of delivery

questions.hint: Questions probe the thinking behind your points.

questions.prompt: You do not have all the facts for a question. Which answer is acceptable?

options.text: Say what more you would need and why
Invent facts that sound plausible
Say you cannot answer without full information
Say it is an unfair question

questions.hint: Show how you would find out.

questions.prompt: Is specialist knowledge usually required for a general presentation exercise?

options.text: Only for senior staff
Not usually, unless the role is technical
Never, in any role
Always, whatever the role

questions.hint: The behaviours are the focus.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible way to prepare for a presentation?

options.text: Memorise a long script word for word
Read slides silently
Skip practice
Practise out loud with a timer

questions.hint: Practice builds timing and confidence.

questions.prompt: How should you start a short presentation?

options.text: Apologise for being nervous
Ask the panel what they would like to hear
Say briefly what you will cover
Read the title slowly

questions.hint: A short opening orients the panel.
